The edge of this place is like a point of no return. Once light goes past it, it cannot get back out to us. A light beam can go in, but it cannot come back out. You can think of the edge as a one-way line. It is not a wall that you can see or touch. Far away, a black hole pulls just like any other thing with the same amount of stuff. If the Sun were made into a black hole, it would have to fit in a ball just a few miles wide. Its pull far away would stay the same. Its strange effects are strongest when you get close.

Its outer edge is called the event horizon. Think of it as a point of no return for light. The horizon is not a solid surface like the ground. The most extreme effects of its gravity show up close to the hole.

According to general relativity, mass and energy bend spacetime, the combined fabric of space and time. Near a black hole, this bending is so strong that light cannot escape. The boundary of the trapped region is called the event horizon. This boundary is not a solid surface that blocks light. A black hole is a region of spacetime from which no signal can reach a distant observer. In general relativity, mass and energy curve spacetime. When a spherical, uncharged object is compressed within its Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, an event horizon forms: no light or other signal can escape from inside it. For an object with the Sun’s mass, that radius is about three kilometers. This radius describes the size of the horizon, not a solid surface. It scales directly with mass, so doubling the mass doubles the radius for the same idealized case. The familiar picture of an escape speed equal to the speed of light at the horizon is a useful comparison, though the horizon is defined by the paths signals can follow in curved spacetime. Far away, a black hole pulls like any other object of the same mass; its extreme effects occur close to the horizon.

Fusion builds an iron core, but iron fusion releases no energy. When the core passes a critical mass, electron pressure can no longer hold it up. This pressure comes from the way electrons behave when matter is packed very tightly. It collapses at a large fraction of light speed. The collapse can leave a dense remnant made largely of neutrons. If the remnant is heavier than about two to three Suns, even neutrons cannot support it, and it becomes a black hole. A lighter remnant may remain as a neutron star rather than collapse further. Fusion builds an iron core, but fusing iron cannot release energy. Once the core exceeds the Chandrasekhar limit, electron degeneracy pressure can no longer support it, and it collapses at a large fraction of light speed. The limit marks the mass above which electron degeneracy pressure alone cannot hold up such a core. This pressure arises from quantum restrictions on how closely electrons can be packed. If the remnant exceeds roughly two to three solar masses, neutron degeneracy pressure also fails, and collapse continues to a black hole. A less massive remnant may instead survive as a neutron star. Supermassive black holes grow over cosmic time by accreting matter and merging. Accretion adds surrounding matter, while mergers combine black holes into a more massive remnant.

All paths lead in. Even a beam of light must go in, not out. A person falling in would not feel a bump at that edge. It would not be like a boat bumping into a dock. The pull of the black hole can still hurt a person, though. The edge marks a point of no return. A black hole can have more or less mass. One with more mass can have a wider edge. A black hole can also spin. Spin pulls its edge in and makes a zone just outside it. In that zone, nothing can stay still when seen from far away.

The event horizon is a causal boundary, not a solid surface; no signal from inside it can escape to the outside. The boundary concerns the possible paths of light and matter, rather than the presence of a physical layer. For a black hole that does not spin, it lies at the Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, about three kilometers per solar mass. For example, a non-spinning black hole with ten solar masses has a horizon about thirty kilometers from its center. Inside, all paths into the future, even those of light, lead inward. This inward direction is unavoidable, not a consequence of an engine running out of fuel. A freely falling observer would notice nothing special at the crossing. Spin shrinks the horizon and creates an outer region called the ergosphere, where nothing can stay still relative to distant stars. Outside the horizon, escape from the ergosphere remains possible, even though objects there must move with the hole's rotation.

The event horizon is a global causal boundary, not a material surface: events inside it cannot send signals to distant observers. Its location depends on the future development of spacetime, rather than on a locally detectable layer of matter. For a non-rotating black hole, the horizon lies at the Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, about three kilometers per solar mass. A Schwarzschild black hole of ten solar masses thus has a horizon radius of approximately thirty kilometers. Inside, future-directed light cones constrain all causal trajectories, including those of light, to decreasing radius. This constraint cannot be overcome by acceleration. A freely falling observer experiences nothing locally special at the crossing. At fixed mass, rotation shrinks the horizon and produces an exterior ergosphere, where nothing can remain stationary relative to distant stars. Frame dragging forces objects there to move in the direction of the hole's spin, but escape from the ergosphere remains possible.

Its definition depends on the entire future of the spacetime and cannot generally be established by a local measurement at the horizon. For a Schwarzschild black hole, the horizon lies at $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, about three kilometers per solar mass. The Schwarzschild radius is an areal radius, defined by the area of a symmetry sphere. Inside, future-directed light cones constrain all causal trajectories, including those of light, to decreasing areal radius; a freely falling observer finds nothing locally special at the crossing. This causal restriction applies regardless of the acceleration available to the observer. At fixed mass, Kerr rotation shrinks the horizon and creates an ergosphere outside it, where nothing stays fixed relative to distant stars. Frame dragging enforces co-rotation there, although future-directed causal trajectories can still escape from the ergosphere.
